name: Uriage

lead: Uriage is a French pharmacy skincare brand associated with thermal spring water from Uriage-les-Bains, a spa town in the Isere region. People use its products for gentle cleansing and hydration, and for sensitive or acne-prone skin, aiming for calmer, clearer-looking skin.
Laboratory studies have looked at Uriage thermal water's effect on immune cells and on acne-associated bacteria.

paras: Users add Uriage cleansers, thermal water mists and moisturizers to a daily routine, as with other drugstore-style skincare lines.
Cosmetic skincare carries a low risk, mainly irritation or allergy to an ingredient; patch-testing guidance on labels applies.

lead: Uriage is a French pharmacy skincare brand drawing on the thermal waters of Uriage-les-Bains. People use it for cleansing, hydration and calming irritated or acne-prone skin. [1][2]

Wikipedia describes Uriage-les-Bains as a spa town in Isere, where the Romans built baths and where the sulphide-and-salt water is used in showers, baths and other treatments. [1] A 19th-century history article notes that physician Adrien Doyon, who translated Hebra's work into French, ran a dermatology practice in Uriage. [2]

In laboratory work, a 1998 study found Uriage spring water induced apoptosis of IL-5-primed human eosinophils in vitro, linked to its calcium content. [3] A 2019 study found Uriage thermal water slowed growth of acneic C. acnes strains and showed anti-biofilm activity against C. acnes and S. aureus. [4]

paras: The spring water of Uriage-les-Bains contains sulphide and salt; Wikipedia says its concentration is similar to blood serum. [1] 19th-century dermatologists such as Alibert and Cazenave used mineral waters in treatment. [2]

Uriage water at over 20% concentration induced eosinophil apoptosis in vitro, an effect mimicked by calcium. [3] In vitro, Uriage thermal water reduced biomass of acneic C. acnes and had antibiofilm effects. [4]
No studies found. The research above is in vitro.
